item.title: Sugar, Soda, and Mental Illness
item.description:
Diet

Sugar, Soda, and Mental Illness

Soda may be contributing to mental illness.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Independent research links soda to obesity and diabetes.
  • Of 60 studies on sugary drinks and disease, every study funded by the beverage industry found no link.
  • Diabetes, obesity, and depression are closely linked, and soda can worsen all three.
Coca-Cola
Source: Melike B/Pexels

In my last post, Diet Soda and the Brain, I described how artificial sweeteners like sucralose may affect hunger, memory, and gut-brain signaling. That raised an obvious question: If diet soda isn't the safe choice we thought, what about regular soda?

The evidence against sugar-sweetened beverages is even more consistent, and has been for years. The more interesting story is why so many of us remain unsure of that. Some of that uncertainty didn't happen by accident. It was manufactured.

What the Independent Science Shows

Sugar-sweetened beverages are the largest source of added sugar in the American diet. A systematic review conducted for the 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans concluded that these drinks may raise the risk of type 2 diabetes in adults, based on studies published between 2000 and 2024. A separate 2025 review found the pattern wasn't subtle: The more sugar-sweetened beverages people drank, the higher their diabetes risk climbed.

This makes biological sense. Sugary drinks deliver a large, fast dose of fructose and glucose with none of the fiber or protein that would normally slow absorption. Over time, that pattern causes weight gain, insulin resistance, and elevated triglycerides — the same factors that lead to type 2 diabetes.

A Pattern Too Consistent to Be Coincidence

In 2016, Dr. Dean Schillinger of UCSF led a review of 60 studies published between 2001 and 2016 on sugary drinks, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. The pattern was undeniable: 34 studies found a link, and only one of those was industry-funded. All 26 studies finding no link were funded by the beverage industry. “This industry seems to be manipulating contemporary scientific processes to create controversy and advance their business interests at the expense of the public's health,” the authors concluded.

That wasn't an isolated finding. A separate analysis in PLOS Medicine found industry-funded beverage studies were roughly five times more likely to find no link between sugary drinks and weight gain than independently funded ones. A skew this consistent, across years and research teams, stops looking like coincidence.

The Playbook

It isn't just which studies get funded, it's which messages get amplified. In 2015, internal documents revealed Coca-Cola had funded and helped shape the Global Energy Balance Network, a group whose public message emphasized exercise over diet, deflecting attention from sugar's role in weight gain. Coca-Cola reportedly helped choose its leadership and messaging while internally calling it a “weapon” in a “war” with public health advocates. The network dissolved once this came to light.

A Boston University study found that between 2011 and 2015, Coca-Cola and PepsiCo funded 96 national health organizations while at the same time lobbying against at least 28 public health bills aimed at reducing consumption of soda. As Schillinger put it: “We are in a public health war with diabetes right now. In every war there is propaganda... we are being played.” The American Beverage Association states that its scientific research mission is to “inform and clarify discussion through scientific inquiry held to the highest standards of integrity.” Although industry funding doesn't automatically invalidate a study, it does raise suspicion when a study's conclusions correlate so reliably with those of the industry that paid for it.

The Mental Health Connection

There's another piece of this story that doesn't get talked about enough: diabetes, obesity, and mental health are closely linked, and each one can make the others worse. Research shows that people with depression are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes, and people with type 2 diabetes are more likely to become depressed. Scientists think this happens because diabetes, obesity, and mental illness all involve some of the same problems inside the body, including ongoing inflammation and stress hormones that stay elevated for too long. The connection is even stronger in people with serious mental illnesses like schizophrenia, who develop type 2 diabetes two to five times more often than the general population, partly because some medications used to treat these illnesses cause weight gain and directly affect blood sugar. Sugary drinks exacerbate the problem. By raising the risk of obesity and diabetes, they may also be raising the risk of mental illness.

Putting It Together

A bigger picture is emerging, one larger than any single sweetener. Diet soda may quietly reshape hunger signals and brain chemistry while regular soda drives obesity, diabetes, and possibly mental illness. The evidence for these links is supported by decades of research. And for just as long, the beverage industry has conducted a well-funded effort to keep the public in the dark.

This doesn't mean every soda drinker will develop diabetes, or that every industry-funded study is worthless. But it does mean that when evaluating claims about sugar and health, it's worth asking who funded the study and what they had to gain. In the meantime, the most reliable way to support your physical and mental health is to focus on water, whole foods, and occasional treats. You don’t have to be rigid about this, but you may find the effort is well worth the benefits.

item.title: Why Emotional Neglect Leaves Life Feeling Pointless
item.description:
Emotions

Why Emotional Neglect Leaves Life Feeling Pointless

One of the most painful effects of emotional neglect is also the most fixable.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional neglect can leave you wondering whether your life has any real purpose or meaning.
  • Two things are shown by research to make life feel meaningful: your emotions and relationships.
  • You can begin to feel that your life matters by welcoming your emotions back in.
Source: pikselstock/StockAdobe

Who hasn't, at some moments of their life, wondered what it's all for?

What's the point?

Why am I here?

What am I supposed to be doing?

Does anything really matter?

I have noticed that some people struggle more than others with these questions.

And I've also realized that there seems to be something about growing up emotionally neglected that predisposes people even more to this struggle.

"But what could that possibly be?" you may be wondering, just as I have wondered for years.

Today, I'd like to share my best answers to all of these questions. I don't claim to know the meaning of life. But I can surely talk about what makes life feel meaningful.

2 Things That Make Life Feel Meaningful

Most psychologists, I think, would agree that two key factors make life feel meaningful, and both are supported by research:

  • Your Emotions: Your emotions drive, motivate, direct, and inspire you. The most memorable moments in your life are the ones in which you feel something. Awed, sad, overwhelmed, shocked, delighted, or disappointed, these moments lodge themselves in your memory. When you feel an emotion, whether it's pleasant or unpleasant, you feel real. Feeling a feeling is a way of feeling alive. Emotions tell you that what is happening matters. They carry with them the message "this matters."
  • Your Relationships: Study after study has shown that it's your connections to others that both anchor and stimulate you. Who is there for you when things get rough? Who's present to celebrate with you and console you? To care for you and be cared for by you? These kinds of connections create the substance that makes life worth living.

These two important life factors offer keys to the struggle for purpose and meaning that many emotionally neglected people experience. When your feelings are under-validated as a child (childhood emotional neglect), you grow up pushing away, questioning, or numbing out your own emotions. This leads to 3 particular challenges when it comes to feeling, as an adult, that your life is meaningful.

  • You are out of touch with your feelings: This undermines your search for meaning in 3 important ways: First, it leaves you feeling, on some level, that you're not fully alive. Second, the feelings that should be informing you about what matters to you are not available enough. And finally, feelings are a source of passion and direction, so a shortage of these messages from within may leave you feeling lost and alone.
  • Your relationships are overly one-sided: Emotional neglect leaves you more focused on caring for others. You give more in your relationships than you're able to take. Your giving nature warms you and moves you, but its one-way nature may limit the depth of your relationships. And it may simply not be quite enough.
  • You feel that you don't matter: The unspoken message you received in childhood was, "Your feelings don't matter." But since your emotions are the most deeply personal part of who you are, what your child self heard was, "You don't matter." As an adult, this message undermines your feelings of life purpose and meaning. After all, if you don't matter, how can your life matter?

The Fix

What's the best fix for all of this? Welcome your emotions back into your life.

I have seen over and over again that three deceptively simple steps can make a huge difference in how important your life feels to you.

  • Try to feel: This may sound strange, but it actually works. Making an effort to have an emotion will start to yield results. You will start to feel more.
  • Tune in to your feelings: Chances are, you're having feelings all the time, but you are simply not aware of them. All it takes is focusing your attention more on what you're feeling. Several times a day, pause, focus your attention inward, and ask yourself, "What am I feeling right now?"
  • Increase your feeling word vocabulary: An important part of getting in touch with your feelings is being able to put words to them. You can find an exhaustive Emotion Word List online to help.

I know it may be hard to believe, but to me, it's abundantly clear: The fuel of life is feeling. If we're not filled up in childhood, we must fill ourselves as adults. Otherwise, we will find ourselves running on empty.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com

item.title: When Your Employee Tries to Outsmart You
item.description:
Leadership

When Your Employee Tries to Outsmart You

When dealing with a sly employee, try these tips to maintain or regain control.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Some employees may make it their mission to outsmart you.
  • Set clear boundaries and expectations while also asking questions to uncover the reasons for their actions.
  • Where appropriate, ask for their input and really listen to their suggestions.
  • Maintain accountability and reward positive behavior consistently.
Source: Gustavo Fring / Pexels

Some employees are sly and cunning, and you may feel that they are trying to outsmart you. You wonder why they are so evasive, shifty, or crafty.

Interestingly, workers you perceive as sly may really be shy, reluctant to ask for better assignments or for more responsibility. They would rather be clever than pushy. They may feel left out, ignored, and not a part of what is going on around the office. They do what is asked but feel that their opinions do not count or hold much weight.

Some employees who feel this way decide to act out in order to get noticed, but they do so in a clever manner. They are ingenious at creating problems for the sole purpose of being praised for their brilliance in solving them.

What You Are Thinking: Glenda is clever and her work is great. But I must wonder if she’s resorting to deception. This morning was a good example. How did that contract with the client get so twisted that Glenda had to jump in to straighten it out? She may be trying to outwit me. I’m going to have a frank talk with her to find out what she’s thinking.

Your Employee’s Thoughts: Well, I guess I’m not getting anywhere in this organization. The best jobs are still going to those who have been here the longest. Good work isn’t enough to get noticed. Where can I spark a little calamity so the boss can see for himself how handy I am when it comes to resolving difficulties?

Sly employees are clever. Your goal is to put their quick thinking and shrewdness to work for you, not against you.

  1. Plan more discussion when you give feedback. Throw them a challenge to find and fill gaps in the process. Let them know that you value their perspective.
  2. Establish a better recognition system. Give them the credit they have earned and be sincere with your praise. You may need to give more frequent praise, after each step, or tie accomplishments to financial incentives or paid time off.
  3. Help workers move out of their one-specialty rut. Tie training to personal goals and ambitions. Give them time each day to brainstorm and think creatively. Offer cross-training opportunities so they can learn more about different yet related jobs within the company.
  4. Keep your people informed. Tell them what other departments are doing. Explain how their work fits into the total picture and why their efforts make a difference.
  5. Reinforce positive behavior. State the problem and explain what has to change in measurable terms. Record progress and praise good results. Be consistent and stick to your word.

You can then ask, How do you feel about the comments I made about your work? or, Yes, I see how that causes difficulty. You know, I really depend on you. How do you think you should solve the problem?

People who try to outsmart you often feel like outsiders. Bridge the gap. They will stop playing tricks if you invite them in and let them be part of what is going on.

item.title: Is Family Enmeshment Really Pathological?
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Is Family Enmeshment Really Pathological?

Research increasingly suggests enmeshment may not be the risk we thought it was.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Family closeness is not universally pathological. It may reflect different cultural ways of relating.
  • The same family behaviour can arise from very different psychological and cultural processes.
  • Instead of asking "Is this enmeshment?", ask, "What system is organising this relationship?"

One of the most enduring ideas in psychotherapy is that healthy families have clear emotional boundaries. When family members become "too close," therapists often worry about enmeshment—relationships in which autonomy is blurred and individuality is compromised.

But what if the problem is not closeness itself? What if we have mistaken one cultural way of organizing relationships for a universal psychological truth?

The evidence keeps becoming more uncomfortable. For decades, Western family therapy has regarded enmeshment as a risk factor. Yet the evidence is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with this assumption.

An Italian study found that while enmeshment predicted poorer wellbeing in the UK, it did not carry the same psychological cost in Italy.

A more recent study of Korean immigrant families found something even more surprising: Children in more enmeshed families actually demonstrated better socioemotional functioning, particularly when families retained stronger heritage cultural values.

Meanwhile, a systematic review of Asian students living in English-speaking countries concluded that many traditional family risk factors simply did not behave as expected. Instead, eating difficulties were more consistently associated with intergenerational cultural conflict and achievement pressures than with family closeness itself. (3 papers, see reference list)

Most researchers conclude that culture moderates psychological phenomena. They argue that enmeshment means different things in different cultures. That is undoubtedly an important insight, but I believe it only gets us halfway. My argument is one step further. I believe the more fundamental questions are: What if different cultures are not simply interpreting the same relationships differently? What if they are organising relationships differently from the beginning?

This is where I believe psychotherapy needs to move next.

When we ask whether enmeshment is adaptive in one culture but maladaptive in another, we are still assuming that everyone is experiencing the same psychological phenomenon.

That assumption may itself be incorrect. Because we may be observing different predictive systems. Our brain is wired to work with predictions, not reactions. (For more, listen to Lisa Feldman Barrett's 10-minute brief explanation.)

In my recent work, I proposed that culture functions as a predictive infrastructure. (Also see reference list.) Culture does not merely influence our beliefs. It shapes what becomes emotionally salient, what feels safe, what requires attention, and even how bodily experiences become recognized as emotions. In short, culture shapes what we feel and what we think we should feel.

From this perspective, two families may appear equally "close." Yet the psychological processes organising that closeness may be fundamentally different. One family's closeness may emerge from fear of separation. Another's may emerge from mutual obligation. And still another's from deeply internalised relational identity.

It can be externally similar, but internally organised in entirely different ways.

When therapists observe only behaviour, they naturally classify families by what they see. But therapy is not ultimately about behaviour. It is about understanding the processes generating behaviour. Because we cannot separate the emotional world from the cultural world.

The question therefore shifts from, "Is this family enmeshed?" to "What psychological system is producing this pattern of closeness?"

That is a profoundly different clinical question.

Consider a daughter who phones her mother every day. One therapist might immediately wonder about dependency. Another might see healthy attachment. Neither conclusion can be drawn from behaviour alone.

The same daily phone call may represent:

  • fear of abandonment
  • reciprocal care
  • cultural obligation
  • relational gratitude
  • simple family habit

The behaviour is identical. The process is not. This is why culturally responsive psychotherapy requires more than cultural knowledge. It requires curiosity about how emotional experience itself has been organised.

Rather than asking, "Is this relationship healthy?" we might begin by asking, "How has this person learned that relationships work?"

Only then can we distinguish genuine pathology from culturally meaningful ways of being connected.

My Invitation

Perhaps the question has never really been whether enmeshment is good or bad. The more important question is whether our diagnostic labels have been describing surface patterns while overlooking the deeper psychological systems that generate them.

If that is true, then culture does not simply change the meaning of family relationships. It changes the very processes through which relationships, emotions, and identity are constructed—and that may be the next frontier for psychotherapy.
